title: Harmonic Circles
description: Learn the repeating four-chord circles behind hundreds of songs, with inline diagrams for every chord.

intro: Shuffle through any ukulele songbook and the same short chord loops keep reappearing — in folk songs and pop hits, hymns and jingles. These loops are called **harmonic circles**: progressions that cycle around and land back where they started. Learn a few circles and you can play hundreds of songs.

This chapter teaches all twenty-four circles — the twelve major-key circles (C, G, F, B flat, D, A, E flat, A flat, E, B, D flat, and F sharp) plus their twelve minor-key twins from C minor to B minor — with every diagram on the page, plus practice drills, strumming patterns, and real songs to try them with. All you need is standard tuning (G–C–E–A).
Each major circle below ends with a **Songs to try** box — real recordings you can play along with as soon as the shapes feel steady.

sections.heading: What Is a Harmonic Circle?
paragraphs: A **harmonic circle** is a progression designed to repeat: the end flows straight back into the beginning, so you can loop it as long as you like. Strum the loop once for an introduction; loop it for three minutes and you have a song.

Circles run on **tension and release**. Some chords feel settled, like sitting down; others lean forward, asking to resolve. When the last chord hands you back to the first, you feel a small click of arrival — and the urge to go around again. **Try it now**: strum C for four slow beats, G for four, then C again. That pull back home is the engine of every circle in this chapter.

Musicians number circle chords with **scale degrees** in Roman numerals: in the key of C, C is **I** (“one”) and A minor is **vi** (“six”). Uppercase means major, lowercase means minor. The most famous circle — C, A minor, F, G — is **I–vi–IV–V**, and those numerals describe the same circle in every key.

sections.heading: Circle in C — the 50s Progression
paragraphs: If you learn one circle, learn **C – A minor – F – G**. It carried hundreds of 1950s ballads — the *50s progression* — and still drives pop, worship, and film music today. On ukulele it is gentle: C and A minor each need one finger, F needs two. When the loop feels smooth, try singing over it — the 50s progression forgives almost any melody.
**Songs to try**: *Stand by Me*, *Blue Moon*, and *Unchained Melody* all ride the I–vi–IV–V loop. Pick one recording, transpose to C, and strum one slow bar per chord — feel the G pull you home.
Notice how the G chord at the end leans forward, almost pulling your hand back to C. That pull is the dominant V chord doing its centuries-old job.
Loop the sequence without pausing between rounds — one slow bar of four strums per chord:

progressions.name: Circle in C — the 50s progression

sections.heading: Circle in G — the Singing Key
paragraphs: Move the same I–vi–IV–V idea to G: **G – E minor – C – D**. The chords ring bright, and the key sits well for most voices with no capo needed. E minor and D are the new shapes here — give the Em fret-2-to-4 stretch and D's three-finger stack a day or two and they settle in.

**Songs to try**: the chorus of Ed Sheeran's *Perfect* loops G–Em–C–D with a capo on 1 (recorded in Ab) — capo up and strum along with the recording. *Stand by Me* fits here too if you transpose it up to G.
Isolate the least familiar change first — E minor to C, a dozen slow loops — then run the full circle:

progressions.name: Circle in G — the singing key

sections.heading: Circle in F — Meeting B Flat
paragraphs: The third circle lives in F: **F – D minor – B flat – C**. F is warm and beginner-friendly, and this circle introduces B flat in the gentlest company: one index mini-barre across E and A at fret 1, middle and ring covering C and G.
**Songs to try**: *Earth Angel* is the classic doo-wop I–vi–IV–V — transpose its loop to F. Then search video sites for an “F D minor B flat C backing track” and take a full chorus over it.
D minor is the darkest chord in this chapter — hear how the circle shadows on D minor, brightens through B flat, and lands home on C moving back to F.
Keep the thumb relaxed, roll the index finger slightly onto its side, and let hand weight — not a squeeze — fret the barre:

progressions.name: Circle in F — meeting B flat

sections.heading: Circle in Bb — Flat-Key Fluency
paragraphs: B flat was the newcomer in F — now it is home. The circle in B flat runs **B flat – G minor – E flat – F**, and its two new shapes share a skeleton: the G string rings open and the index holds the A string's first fret in both. G minor stacks the middle on the C string's second fret and the ring on the E string's third fret; E flat keeps the ring on the E string's third fret and moves only the middle up to the C string's third fret.

**Songs to try**: transpose *Earth Angel* up to B flat — doo-wop loves flat keys — then search video sites for a “B flat G minor E flat F backing track” and ride a full chorus. Jazz players live in these keys, so this circle opens standards next.
Use the built-in pivot: B flat to G minor keeps the middle on the C string's second fret and the index on the A string's first fret — move only the other fingers, then run the full circle:

progressions.name: Circle in Bb — flat-key fluency

sections.heading: Circle in D — Your First Barre
paragraphs: The circle in D — **D – B minor – G – A** — is the busker's key: bright, loud, and made for singing over. D stacks three fingers across the second fret — index, middle, and ring on the G, C, and E strings while the A rings open — and A needs just two fingers on the top strings. The price of admission is B minor, your first full barre: the index lays across the C, E, and A strings at the second fret while the ring reaches the G string's fourth fret.

**Songs to try**: transpose *Stand by Me* to D and strum it like a street performer. Then search for a “D B minor G A backing track” and take the verse. If B minor buzzes, roll the index onto its bony edge and drop the thumb low behind the neck.
Isolate the hard move first: loop D to B minor slowly — the C and E strings stay at the second fret, only the fingers change — a dozen times, then run the full circle:

progressions.name: Circle in D — your first barre

sections.heading: Circle in A — Stand by Me's Home Key
paragraphs: Here is the payoff: *Stand by Me* was recorded in A, so **A – F-sharp minor – D – E** lets you play along with the original record, in the original key. A is an easy two-finger shape, and F-sharp minor simply keeps both fingers where they are and adds the ring on the E string's second fret.

**Songs to try**: put on the Ben E. King recording and strum A–F#m–D–E along with the band. The hurdle is E major, one of the hardest shapes in this chapter: the index holds the A string's second fret while the middle, ring, and pinky climb the G, C, and E strings at the fourth fret. Give it its own one-minute drill before joining the loop.
Loop A to F-sharp minor until the added ring finger lands clean, fold in D and E one at a time, then run the full circle:

progressions.name: Circle in A — Stand by Me's home key

sections.heading: Circle in Eb — Motown Soul
paragraphs: Soul and Motown live in E flat: **E flat – C minor – A flat – B flat**. E flat and B flat are old friends from the B-flat circle; the newcomers are C minor — G string open, three fingers stacked across the third fret on the C, E, and A strings — and A flat, the biggest stretch yet: the index barres the C and A strings at the third fret while the middle takes the E string's fourth fret and the ring reaches the G string's fifth fret.

**Songs to try**: transpose *Stand by Me* down to E flat and feel the Motown groove — half that catalog sits in E flat and B flat for the horns. Then search video sites for an “E flat C minor A flat B flat backing track” and ride a full chorus.
Anchor the changes with two index pivots — B flat to E flat keeps the index on the A string's first fret, C minor to A flat keeps the index on the C string's third fret — then run the full circle:

progressions.name: Circle in Eb — motown soul

sections.heading: Circle in Ab — Four-Flat Territory
paragraphs: Four flats deep: **A flat – F minor – D flat – E flat**. A flat and E flat carry over from the last circle; F minor is a gentle stretch — index on the G string's first fret, middle on the E string's first fret, pinky on the A string's third fret, C string open — and D flat is a pinky-reach barre: the index lays across the G, C, and E strings at the first fret while the pinky lands the A string's fourth fret.

**Songs to try**: transpose *Earth Angel* to A flat for a gospel-choir glow, then search for an “A flat F minor D flat E flat backing track”. Jazz and gospel players call these flat keys home — you are learning their language.
Use the G-string anchor: F minor to D flat keeps the index on the G string's first fret — hold it while the other fingers reset — then run the full circle:

progressions.name: Circle in Ab — four-flat territory

sections.heading: Circle in E — Rock's Home Key
paragraphs: Rock's home key: **E – C-sharp minor – A – B**. E major returns from the A circle and A is easy; C-sharp minor pairs the index and middle on the G and C strings' first fret with the pinky stretching to the A string's fourth fret, E string open — and B is a compact barre: index across the E and A strings at the second fret, middle on the C string's third fret, ring on the G string's fourth fret.

**Songs to try**: transpose the 50s progression to E and strum it like a bar-band encore — E, A, and B powered a thousand rock songs. Then search for an “E C sharp minor A B backing track” and take the verse.
Anchor on the A string: B to E keeps the index on the A string's second fret — the rest of the hand rebuilds around it — then run the full circle:

progressions.name: Circle in E — rock's home key

sections.heading: Circle in B — Five-Sharp Summit
paragraphs: Five sharps up: **B – G-sharp minor – E – F-sharp**. B and E carry over from the last circle; G-sharp minor uses all four fingers — index on the G string's first fret, middle on the A string's second fret, ring on the C string's third fret, pinky on the E string's fourth fret — and F-sharp is a stretch-barre: the index covers the C and A strings at the first fret, the middle takes the E string's second fret, and the ring reaches the G string's third fret.

**Songs to try**: transpose *Stand by Me* to B and hear it go glassy and bright — high keys shimmer on the ukulele's small body. Then search for a “B G sharp minor E F sharp backing track” and play a full chorus without stopping.
Trust the pinky: G-sharp minor to E keeps the pinky on the E string's fourth fret — plant it and swing the other fingers home — then run the full circle:

progressions.name: Circle in B — five-sharp summit

sections.heading: Circle in Db — Five-Flat Summit
paragraphs: Five flats deep, the pianist's key: **D flat – B-flat minor – G flat – A flat**. D flat and A flat are old friends, and G flat returns from the B circle; the only newcomer is B-flat minor — a full index barre across the C, E, and A strings at the first fret with the ring on the G string's third fret.

**Songs to try**: transpose *Earth Angel* down to D flat for late-night warmth — worship pianists live in D flat because the black-key shapes sit under the hands. Then search for a “D flat B flat minor G flat A flat backing track” and take a full chorus.

This circle barely moves the hand: B-flat minor to G flat keeps the ring on the G string's third fret and the index barre on the C and A strings' first fret — just add the middle on the E string's second fret — then run the full circle:

progressions.name: Circle in Db — five-flat summit

sections.heading: Circle in F# — The Final Frontier
paragraphs: The twelfth and final key: **F-sharp – D-sharp minor – B – C-sharp**. (The diagrams spell three of them the flat way — G flat, E-flat minor, D flat — same pitches, same fingers.) Everything is familiar except D-sharp minor, and even it is friendly: all four fingers in a descending staircase — ring on the G string's third fret, pinky on the C string's third fret, middle on the E string's second fret, index on the A string's first fret.

**Songs to try**: the victory lap — transpose *Stand by Me* to F-sharp, then play all twelve major keys in a row, C to F-sharp, one chorus each. Search for an “F sharp D sharp minor B C sharp backing track” to close out the set.

Three fingers never move: F-sharp to D-sharp minor keeps the ring on the G string's third fret, the middle on the E string's second fret, and the index on the A string's first fret — only the C string changes hands — then run the full circle:

progressions.name: Circle in F# — the final frontier

sections.heading: Minor Circles in C–Eb
paragraphs: Flip a circle to its darker twin: in a minor key the home chord is minor, and the loop runs **i – VI – III – VII**. In A minor that is A minor – F – C – G — the same four shapes as C's circle, starting from a different home.

The twelve loops below are the minor twin of the major set — one canonical circle per minor key. Open any of them in the explorer to see all seven diatonic chords, including the diminished chord on the second degree.

progressions.name: Circle in C minor — the relative's turn
Circle in C# minor — a half step up
Circle in D minor — the saddest key
Circle in Eb minor — six flats deep

sections.heading: Minor Circles in E–G
paragraphs: The middle four minor keys keep the same i – VI – III – VII loop. Notice how many shapes you already know: E minor's circle is C, G, D, and E minor — four old friends in a new order.

progressions.name: Circle in E minor — the guitarist's minor
Circle in F minor — four flats down
Circle in F# minor — relative of A
Circle in G minor — two flats down

sections.heading: Minor Circles in G#–B
paragraphs: The final four minor keys, including A minor — the most-played minor key of all, home to *Stairway to Heaven*, *House of the Rising Sun*, and half the singer-songwriter shelf. Run all twelve minor loops back to back to close out the set.

progressions.name: Circle in G# minor — relative of B
Circle in A minor — the people's minor
Circle in Bb minor — five flats deep
Circle in B minor — relative of D

sections.heading: Practicing Circles Cleanly
paragraphs: Knowing the chords is half the skill; the other half is *changing* between them without breaking time. Practice the changes, not just the grips — a chord you can form in five seconds is not yet a chord you can play.

Start with the **slow-change drill**: loop two neighboring chords back and forth, one strum each, keeping every note ringing. Buzz or mute? Slow down instead of squeezing — clean tone at half speed becomes clean tone at full speed within days.

Next, learn to see **pivot fingers**: fingers that stay put, or barely move, between two shapes. From A minor to F, your middle finger stays planted on the G string's second fret — just add the index on the E string's first fret. From F to D minor, both fingers stay exactly where they are while you add a finger on the C string's second fret. From D minor to B flat, your index finger stays on the E string's first fret and extends across the A string, while the C string stays fretted at the second fret. The first new circles hide pivots too: A to F-sharp minor keeps both fingers while the ring joins on the E string's second fret, and B flat to G minor keeps the middle on the C string's second fret and the index on the A string's first fret. The sharp and flat keys hide anchors of their own: B to E keeps the index on the A string's second fret, C minor to A flat keeps the index on the C string's third fret, and F-sharp to D-sharp minor holds three fingers while only the C string changes hands. Naming your pivots turns four separate grips into one connected hand dance.

When the shapes feel familiar, run this ladder:

- **One-minute changes**: one pair, sixty seconds, count clean changes. Beat it tomorrow.
- **Metronome ladder**: full circle at 60 bpm, one strum per beat; climb to 70, then 80 when flawless.
- **Island strum**: down, down-up, up, down-up — one pattern per chord.
- **Song run**: play a full verse and chorus of one song from this chapter without stopping, mistakes and all.
Five focused minutes a day on one circle beats an hour of distracted strumming — fingers build their memory while you sleep, so short daily sessions work remarkably well.

sections.heading: Hearing Circles in Songs
paragraphs: Once a circle lives in your fingers, you *hear* it everywhere. Put on *Stand by Me*, count its four repeating bass stations, and strum I–vi–IV–V along in the same key. At first you will fumble the timing; within a few songs you will catch the changes earlier and earlier. Then try *Perfect* and *Blue Moon* — and *Stand by Me* in its original key of A.

Make it a game: **name that circle**. Play a 50s or doo-wop playlist and call out “circle” or “not it” inside the first verse. Check yourself by strumming along — catching the V chord leaning home a bar early means your ear is working.

The twelve major circles in this chapter cover every major key. Sibling loops — I–V–vi–IV (*Let It Be*, *No Woman No Cry*), the 12-bar blues, the Andalusian descent — reuse the same listening skill. Master these twelve and you hold the key to them all.

summary: You now know what harmonic circles are — repeating loops built on tension and release — and can play all twelve major circles: the 50s progression in C, the singing circle in G, the warm circle in F, flat-key B flat, big D with your first barre, A — home of *Stand by Me* — plus E flat, A flat, E, B, D flat, and F sharp to complete the set.

Keep the habit small: five minutes of slow changes, one metronome climb, and one song played by ear each week. When a fingering slips, the Chords reference holds every diagram — and the next time four chords sound pleasantly familiar, you will know why.
The chapter's second half adds the twelve minor-key twins — one i–VI–III–VII loop per minor key, from C minor to B minor — each with its own diatonic table in the explorer.
